core: Operators are symbols that perform an operation on one or more operands and produce a result value.
Arithmetic operators: + - * / % // (and ** for exponentiation), including the distinction between true division (/) and floor division (//), and modulo (%).
Comparison/relational operators: == != < > <= >=, which evaluate to boolean values.
Assignment operators: = for binding a value to a variable, and compound/augmented forms like += -= *= /=.
Logical operators named here (and, or, not) as the boolean-combining operators, with depth deferred to boolean-logic.
Operator precedence and associativity, with a worked example (2 + 3 * 4 = 14) that would be wrong without correct precedence.
supporting: Left-to-right associativity for most binary operators; right-to-left for ** (exponentiation).
Comparison chaining (x < y <= z) in Python.
Integer vs float division and the sign of the modulo result in Python.
outOfScope: Truth tables, De Morgan's laws, and short-circuit evaluation (owned by boolean-logic).
The full type system and numeric types (owned by data-types).
Declaring and naming variables in depth (owned by variables).
Bitwise operators beyond a passing mention.

claims.claim: An operator is a symbol that performs an operation on one or more operands and yields a result; e.g. in 3 + 4 the + is the operator and 3 and 4 are operands.
Python's arithmetic operators include + - * / // % and **; / always returns a float, // performs floor division discarding the fractional part, and % returns the remainder.
Comparison operators (< <= > >= == !=) have the same precedence and yield boolean results; they can be chained left-to-right, so x < y <= z is equivalent to x < y and y <= z with y evaluated once.

In Python's precedence table, ** binds tighter than the unary +/-/~ and the multiplicative operators (* / // % @), which bind tighter than additive + and -, which bind tighter than comparisons, which bind tighter than not, and, or.
Because * has higher precedence than +, the expression 2 + 3 * 4 evaluates to 14, not 20; parentheses (2 + 3) * 4 force the addition first and give 20.
Most binary operators associate left to right (10 - 3 - 2 == 5), but exponentiation associates right to left, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 == 2 ** (3 ** 2) == 512, not 64.
Augmented assignment operators such as += -= *= //= combine an operation with assignment; x += 3 updates x to its previous value plus 3.
The single = is the assignment operator (binding a value to a name) while == is the equality comparison operator; confusing the two is a common error.

sourceRecords.title: The Python Language Reference — 6. Expressions (Operator precedence)
sourceRecords.notes: Section 6.17 gives the authoritative operator-precedence table (highest to lowest), states that ** groups right-to-left and most operators left-to-right, that comparisons share one precedence level, yield booleans, and chain left-to-right. Used for precedence, associativity, and comparison-chaining claims. Fetched and read the live page 2026-08-19.
